articles.title: Starbucks Workers Are Calling for a Nationwide Boycott
articles.author: Jenny Brown
articles.content: No contract? No Starbucks coffee at the union hall. Seeking to pressure Starbucks to finally sign a contract with its 12,000 unionized baristas, Starbucks Workers United announced a boycott of the chain August 25. In addition to individual customers, they are asking organizations and unions to stop patronizing the coffee giant, including avoiding catering and sponsorships, until they get a contract. The AFL-CIO has already signed on, and the 25,000-strong Chicago Teachers Union voted to boycott on August 26. Starbucks Workers United members conducted their largest and longest strike yet last November, demanding that the company resolve its 550 unfair labor practice charges and negotiate in good faith. Three thousand baristas in one hundred cities struck, in some cases staying out into January. They asked customers to delete their Starbucks phone app and avoid patronizing all stores. The company seemed ready to bargain for a moment, but then went back to stonewalling, baristas said. “They will continue to stonewall and stall for as long as they believe they can get away with it,” said Campbell Marusa, a five-year barista in Greeley, Colorado. Sporadic strikes have continued. August 15–16, workers in California, Missouri, Tennessee, and Pennsylvania walked off the job. The walkouts came during Unicorn Frappuccino weekend, when the stores briefly offered a complicated multicolored drink that spiked sales and exhausted workers. Baristas were told they had to work that weekend and could not take time except for emergencies. In Nashville, baristas walked off August 15 to raise the alarm about a new blending powder the company rolled out in mid-July that became easily airborne and was giving workers sore throats, coughs, and headaches from breathing it. Starbucks baristas have been fighting for a first contract for nearly five years. Workers started an organizing wave with union election wins in Buffalo, New York, in late 2021. Since then, over 700 stores have voted union — affiliating with the Service Employees International Union’s Workers United division — but that’s still fewer than 5 percent of the company’s 16,000 outlets in the United States. To stop the union’s spread, the company has racked up the largest number of unfair labor practices in US history, with 550 still unresolved. Despite well-documented management intimidation, the union continues to grow by several stores a month. Three at All Times A key contract demand is around understaffing. Workers are demanding three people on the floor at all times, and they want available hours to go to current baristas, rather than the company’s prevailing practice of hiring more people and keeping established workers starved for hours. Striking Nashville barista Baylor Baucom told the Nashville Banner that his store sometimes has only two workers. “That’s unacceptable, in my opinion, considering how many different positions we have on our floor — making drinks, making the food, taking orders, taking orders in the drive-through.” Many longer-term baristas report that staffing has worsened in the last five years. “The working conditions and food service are getting worse while prices are getting higher,” said Marusa. Many workers report that even when they are available to work more, managers keep their hours below the number required to receive benefits. Marusa said a coworker in Greeley keeps asking for more hours but is being kept at the minimum. “After asking the manager for more hours, my store manager told her that there are resources to help her budget her money,” said Marusa. “With the hours that she’s getting scheduled, she’s getting paid less than $800 a month. The issue isn’t how she’s budgeting her money; the issue is that she is being chronically underscheduled.” Pay has improved since the union started organizing, but in forty-three states the starting wages are still below $16. The union is asking for $17 an hour starting pay and 4 percent annual raises. Grueling Pace, Angry Customers Because there is not enough staff for the workload, baristas say they are forced to speed up their work to a grueling pace, while customers face long wait times. Customer frustration is absorbed by the workers. “Everyone in my store was being scheduled less than their stated preferred hours because of our ‘labor budget,’” said Marusa. Because of this, workers can’t take sick time, lest they drop below the required hours limit. When a coworker was shoved and stomped by a customer in June, she had to go to the hospital, Marusa said. “Her ribs were bruised, but she came into work the next day.” She couldn’t take time off because she would lose precious hours and risk being fired, said Marusa. The workers want health and safety addressed in the contract, including procedures to protect against assaults by customers. More robust staffing would make attacks less likely, they said. “It honestly affects your mental health sometimes,” Baucom told the Banner , “because you’re understaffed, you’re being told that you need to go faster, and then you turn around and a customer is yelling at you because they’ve been waiting too long.” Another sticking point is the annoying requirement to write something cheery and spontaneous on each cup. Workers face discipline if they don’t do it. One wrote on Reddit that they had been fired for “not including required markings on cups put in handoff plane.” Another responded, “Nothing irks me more when I’m running a shift and I have a callout, I’m supporting on bar and I’m running around doing a million things and my manager approaches me and says ‘there should be no excuses for not writing on cups.’” “Inhaling Drywall Dust” The union chalked a win in mid-August when Starbucks withdrew its new Blending Powder Beverage Mix, used in cold “refresher” drinks, that was making many baristas sick with respiratory symptoms. Many took to social media with their reactions to the powder. The union asked an occupational health professor at the University of Illinois Medical Center, Peter Orris, to evaluate the powder’s ingredients. He found that three of them — gum arabic, xanthan gum, and amorphous silica — are associated with respiratory issues when inhaled. He recommended masking, special ventilation, and special cleanup procedures to handle the product. Workers who have reactions should avoid the product, he wrote. Baristas took to social media to celebrate the product’s withdrawal, commenting “No more inhaling drywall dust!!” and “I can finally breathe on cold bar again,” and “Thank the lord, my asthma was tweaking. . . . It was effecting me so bad but I felt weird saying anything about it at work.” “We need to turn up the pressure,” said Marusa, citing the boycott. She encouraged unions and other organizations to pass a resolution to run “a Starbucks-free organization [and] encourage your community members to boycott Starbucks .”

articles.title: Tony Is a Terrific Coming-of-Age Story
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content: A loose adaptation of just a few pages from the memoir that made Anthony Bourdain famous, Tony is a triumph of warm, earthy, character-centered filmmaking on a modest scale. Writer-director Matt Johnson (BlackBerry, Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie) focuses the film on one fateful summer in 1975, when glowering, disaffected nineteen-year-old Tony Bourdain (Dominic Sessa) gets his start in restaurant work as a lowly dishwasher in a Cape Cod seafood joint.This film will make a great double feature with Alexander Payne’s delightful Christmas movie The Holdovers (2023). Both star the highly talented Dominic Sessa as a troubled teen acting out furiously while coming of age in the 1970s, and both center on brief but intense vacation interludes when a small cluster of characters, pushed together by circumstances, forge unexpectedly important and memorable relationships.The Holdovers is about a group of boarding school kids whose rich parents don’t bring them home for the holidays, leaving them in the charge of a crusty, isolated, misanthropic middle-aged teacher (Paul Giamatti) who gradually becomes an unexpectedly valued mentor. In Tony, the mentor figure is the self-contained middle-aged “Chef” Jose Vatel (Antonio Banderas), who’s the owner of the seafood joint called the Flagship and the representative of the local Portuguese fishing community in Provincetown, whose traditions have waned over time. He employs a motley crew of cooks: charismatic young hard case Sal (Leo Woodall), garrulous shit-stirrer Stavros (Stavros Halkias), and silent, middle-aged, ultracompetent Tyrone (Michael Jibrin).Chef has Tony thrown out of his place for drunken offensiveness — he’s rude to bartender and counter server Mary (Monica Raymund) and actually puts his hand on her arm, which will not be tolerated at the Flagship. Tony gets efficiently bounced out of the place by Sal, who pauses curbside over the unconscious Tony to help himself to all the money in his wallet. Upon seeing Tony passed out in the gutter, Chef relents and allows him to sleep on the hammock strung up on the porch of his beachside home. He also lets Tony earn his keep by washing dishes at the Flagship, which is always frantically busy serving up fishy fast food to summer tourists.Chef’s reasons for helping Tony are initially mysterious, as are many things about him that he doesn’t discuss — his serious religious beliefs, his personal life, his illustrious culinary past, and his habit of rousing Tony from deep sleep every morning by dumping a bucket of seawater over his head as a kind of ultimate wake-up call. But eventually it becomes clear that he does all this for one reason only, the same reason he gives for hiring Sal and presumably all the other kitchen staff members — he likes them. He sees potential in them.And Tony is hard to like. The film opens with a title-card quote from Bourdain’s memoir: “I was — to be frank — a spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive and thoughtless young lout, and badly in need of a good ass-kicking.”Tony is also an insecure liar of such fantastical proportions that he winds up juggling various false accounts of what he’s doing over the summer to his parents, Pierre and Gladys Bourdain (Rich Sommer and Dagmara Domińczyk), his boss Chef, his new workplace friend Sal, and his big high school crush, Nancy (Emilia Jones). We see the development of the lies from the start of the film as Vassar College student Tony presents himself as a bildungsroman-writing wunderkind to a triumvirate of professors in charge of awarding a prestigious writing fellowship. Tony then brags that the fellowship is essentially in the bag to his friend in a local Poughkeepsie bar, and to Nancy, whom he’s trying to impress, and to his parents — most painfully, his observant, judgmental, and undermining mother, who isn’t buying his latest tall tale.All of which makes it awkward when he gets turned down for the fellowship.Refusing to admit the humiliating truth to anyone, he heads off to Cape Cod in pursuit of Nancy, because she said she’d be working there over the summer. When he sees her again on a Provincetown dock, he lies, of course, claiming to have no memory of her mentioning her destination — it’s a mere coincidence that he happens to be there on fellowship, writing his bildungsroman. But Nancy’s already got a boyfriend at the pizza joint where she works, so Tony gets drunk in teenage despair at the Flagship that night, and the rest is history.Tony is impressed by the raucous, profane, high-living, drug-and-liquor-fueled ways of the Flagship’s cooks, Sal and Stavros, and their tough camaraderie in a demanding profession. There are immediate tests of strength and know-how that Tony fails. He’s too weak to pull down the heavy lever of the wall-mounted potato cutter, and when he lies about having cooking experience, he’s immediately exposed as a fake by Sal and Stavros, who tell him to pick up a cast-iron skillet with a handle they know is red-hot. He drops it howling and calling for anti-burn ointment, while Tyrone, with silent contempt, picks up the dropped skillet with his bare, scarred, kitchen-toughened hand.The film is chockablock with great performances. Sessa fulfills his Holdovers promise while raising concerns that he’s already typecast as a miserable, vulnerable, angst-ridden, self-obsessed, overly privileged young bastard who learns to be a decent human being. Antonio Banderas is so good as Chef: so full of quiet, eccentric humor and intense unspoken feeling, he’s almost sure to be nominated for a Best Supporting Actor Oscar, and he’ll have been robbed if he doesn’t get it.But the scene-stealing breakout performance is by British actor Leo Woodall as Sal, a callous, swaggering young American thug so effortlessly magnetic that he’s a real danger to impressionable punks like Tony, who immediately takes him as a role model. He’s also a lure and a menace to every young woman of just-barely-legal age that he meets. Stavros sneers that Sal has the age of consent memorized in every state of the union.For all the macho hijinks and strutting tough-guy attitudes that are central to Tony — as they are to Kitchen Confidential as well — the whole poignancy of the film is about overcoming them in order to grow up and develop sufficient perception, compassion, and ability to appreciate other people that you’re not doing damage to yourself and others absolutely everywhere you go. Anthony Bourdain became an inspirational figure on the political left especially because, for all his early privilege and arrogance, he learned through cooking and eating all sorts of foods made by all sorts of people all over the world, and documenting it, to be a real mensch, respectful and appreciative and discerning.Tony might seem minor as a biopic, concerned as it is with only a sliver of Bourdain’s lifetime experience. But it’s presented as the crucial sliver when he finds an infinitely better way forward. Ironically, it turns out to be quite a wise and touching bildungsroman.

articles.title: Centrist Dems Are at War With Their Own Voters on Israel
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: The “civil war” currently playing out in the Democratic Party is usually thought of as a battle between socialists and progressives on the one hand, and centrists on the other. Which it is. But it’s also a battle between the Democratic establishment and its own voters.If you need proof, look at party leadership’s plans to install Jared Moskowitz and several other right-wing Democrats in influential foreign policy positions if the party retakes the House of Representatives.“I’ll be in a position to help steer US policy on Israel and the Middle East,” said Moskowitz, who will become chair of the Middle East and North Africa subcommittee if the party wins big in November.The views of the Democratic electorate on Israel are not ambiguous. A recent poll carried out by YouGov, for example, found that majorities of upward of 60 percent of Democratic voters across several key states overwhelmingly want their 2028 presidential candidate to cut off weapons for Israel and even sanction Israel over its illegal behavior.Moskowitz’s appointment is, to put it lightly, a slap in the face of this supermajority of his party’s own voters. Moskowitz is a darling of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) for his implacable support for Israel’s genocide, opposing a ceasefire for months while Israeli forces carried out some of the worst killing and vehemently opposing any conditions whatsoever on US aid to Israel — even though, under US law, it’s already illegal to send aid to states violating human rights.At one point, he was one of just sixteen Democrats to join the GOP in voting to reverse former President Joe Biden’s decision to stop sending Israel the largest, most indiscriminately destructive US bombs. At various points, he led a congressional effort to conceal the number of civilians Israel had killed, voted to defund the United Nations (UN) agency responsible for helping Palestinian refugees, and authored a bill to defund the UN if it expelled Israel, which he has introduced multiple times.In fact, it’s fair to say that, if it were up to Moskowitz, he would probably outlaw the views of most of his own party’s voters. He authored a resolution absurdly declaring “From the river to sea” an antisemitic call for violence, and voted to censure his own Democratic colleague, Rashida Tlaib, because she suggested Israel bombed a hospital in Gaza — a hospital that Israel has proceeded to repeatedly bomb in the years since, besides bombing every other hospital in the territory.Since then, he has lent his full support to Donald Trump’s free speech crackdown, supporting Trump’s attempt to deport a green card holder critical of Israel, writing a bill to punish Americans who boycott Israel, and pressuring Trump to retaliate against Colombia because of its president’s criticism of the country, which he did. Before Trump took office, Moskowitz had agitated for a federal crackdown on campus protests that he absurdly likened to white supremacist rallies, another policy that has become a defining feature of Trump’s authoritarian second term.But beyond Israel and Palestine, House Minority Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries’s decision to elevate Moskowitz also hands the party’s Middle East policy to a supporter of what has proven to be Trump’s most disastrous foreign policy decision, both on the politics and its actual outcomes for US interests: the Iran war.In the lead-up to Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu’s first attack on the country last year, Moskowitz described himself as “to the right of this issue to the J. D. Vance-[Steve] Witkoff approach, and I agree, quite frankly, more with Senator Lindsey Graham and probably Senator Tom Cotton.” The fact that he quickly slipped in the claim that he wasn’t calling for bombing was undermined by the fact that bombing Iran was the long-standing position of both Graham and Cotton. Sure enough, Moskowitz put out a press release supporting the Israeli bombing a month later and went on Fox News to defend it.Moskowitz went one further with Trump’s all-out war on Iran this year, which has turned into a six-month-long quagmire that’s caused huge numbers of casualties and made the cost of living spike for US consumers.This time, rather than mere rhetorical support, Moskowitz gave Trump material aid to start the war. He publicly refused to vote for a War Powers Resolution being brought by the bipartisan duo of Ro Khanna and Thomas Massie to prevent Trump from acting on the horrible advice of the dumbest right-wing war hawks, labeling the effort to constrain him “the Ayatollah Protection Act.” It put him on the other side of most of his own party and its top leadership who backed the measure, including Jeffries himself.Having helped Trump get the country into this mess, Moskowitz then predictably took the position that the United States had no choice but to stay in the war as long as possible and get sucked even deeper into it.“Now that we’re there and we’re in this war, we have to get the uranium. We can’t just go home,” he said in June, pointing to the US deaths and other costs that his support for the war made happen.Any deal to end the war — which he totally supports, Moskowitz assured viewers — had to involve Iran dismantling its nuclear sites and handing over its uranium, maximalist demands that would functionally make it impossible for the United States to extricate itself from the war.The fact that Moskowitz and Jeffries were on different sides of the most consequential US foreign policy question of the year (and probably the decade), yet Jeffries has picked him to potentially steer US foreign policy in the region anyway, suggests two things.One is that Jeffries’s support for the War Powers Resolution to prevent Trump’s war was as half-hearted as many critics suspected. Recall that there was already reporting earlier this year that Democratic leaders actually wanted Trump to start a war with Iran, a war they ardently desired but didn’t want to face the political blowback for carrying out themselves.The other is that it points to the role Moskowitz will play for the party’s corporate faction moving forward. Centrists like Jeffries understand that both the Iran war and unconditional US support for Israel are lethally unpopular with voters but are committed to both, partly for ideological reasons and partly because of their alliance with large, pro-Israel donors. By plonking Moskowitz and other Israel First ideologues into these positions, they can let them take the heat for the hawkish foreign policy decisions they secretly favor while publicly posturing that they’re in line with what Democratic voters want.Moskowitz and the rest will play political cover for a leadership that remains out of step with, if not actively hostile to, the will of its own voters. It’s a strategy that will translate into more disastrous foreign policy choices that the rest of the country has to live with — but also only remains viable as long as Moskowitz and the others are able to keep winning their races.

articles.title: Faced With Record Fires, France Skimps on Fire Crews
articles.author: Marlon Ettinger
articles.content: For thirty years, Patrice Hureaux has fought fires in his forest-covered corner of southwestern France. Every summer, he and his team work diligently to put out fires in the woods right as they start. Landes, where he lives and works, is one of the most wooded of France’s 101 local départements , with fully two-thirds of its territory covered in trees. He and his colleagues have their work cut out for them, but the vigilance is worth it. “It’s much easier to put out a fire when it starts than to let it build in intensity,” Hureaux told me earlier this month. “After, you need much more water and much more resources.” This summer has presented a particularly grueling challenge for France’s volunteer firefighters like Hureaux, as well as its understaffed professional forces. Out-of-control fires have swept across stretches of land four times as large as Paris, causing a quarter of a million people to flee their homes, injuring hundreds of firefighters, and leaving four firefighters dead. For months this summer, France groaned under a series of hellish heat waves that at times made parts of the country the hottest places in the world. Temperatures have soared dizzyingly above 105 degrees Fahrenheit, with catastrophic effects for the country’s wildlife — think lakes filled with dead fish and mysterious bird deaths. Nearly everywhere starting in late June, vegetation turned eerily autumnal, with wilting trees shedding amarillo and amber leaves to skitter across sunbaked streets, and springy green grass shriveling into dry, faded-yellow straw. In Landes, Hureaux explained, a rainy autumn, winter, and spring meant that lots of vegetation grew. Ferns and other undergrowth covered the forest floor, then a storm at the end of the winter downed tree branches and soaked the soil. The loose, waterlogged ground made it easy for wind to pull pine trees up and across pathways the firefighters need to access the forest and put out flames before they burn out of control. But from the start of summer, as heat waves rolled in one after another, all this abundant material dried up. By mid-August, it was the perfect fuel for a conflagration that burned nearly two thousand hectares and caused six hundred locals to be evacuated from their homes. As the endless heat waves broke last week, the fires have begun to come under control, and residents have been returned to their homes. But Hureaux is convinced that the new climatic conditions mean that every year could see fires just as frequent and intense. “The forest has changed. There’s no reason to believe it will stop. . . . I think there’ll be more episodes like this. . . . all this has changed our working conditions a little,” Hureaux told me. Quarter-Century Shift According to an analysis by Reporterre , there were thirty times more fires in France by July this year than there had been in all of 2010. Ten times as much land has burned too — at least 119,000 hectares. One hectare is equal to ten thousand square meters — about the size of a Manhattan city block. Reporterre’s analysis, based on a dataset that tracks significant fires of over thirty hectares, shows the dramatic explosion in fires over the past twenty-five years. In 2010 there were nine such fires. As of mid-July this year, there have been 308, outpacing the previous peak of 304 fires, from 2019. Before that past peak, there had never been over a hundred. In the past, the threat of fires has been largely confined to France’s hotter Mediterranean coast and hinterlands. But the national weather service has warned that the projected 4°C rise by the end of the century could create a generalized fire risk across the country, including in the densely populated Paris metropolitan region or the wet banks of the Loire valley. In July, firefighters fought an out-of-control wildfire forty miles south of Paris in the Fontainebleau forest which burned about 10 percent of its surface area. At the same time as these deadly weather conditions are becoming an established feature of the climate, across the national territory, firefighters say that there’s another factor making the situation even worse. They point to a serious shortage in manpower and resources needed to confront the new reality. Megafeux “I don’t like the term ‘mega-fires,’” Rémy Chabbouh told me, referring to a common description of the fires by the French media this summer. A spokesman for the SUD union of professional firefighters, Chabbouh says that the term wrongly implies that there’s nothing that can be done about the fires, casting them as a “diabolic” force of nature. That isn’t the case, Chabbouh, a longtime firefighter himself, insisted. In 2022, a similar wave of massive out-of-control fires swept across France from the Gironde in the South to Brittany in the North. Even the Brocéliande — a misty, moist, moss-covered forest that is the setting of many of the Arthurian legends — went up in flames (this year, access is currently limited because of extreme dryness and the threat of fire). For the first time, all of France was burning at once. Firefighters rung the alarm bell and, after a series of working groups and consultative meetings, put a raft of propositions on the interior minister’s desk in September 2025. In France, the SDIS national firefighting service is under this ministry’s authority. Now, with a budget fight coming early next month, Chabbouh says the proposals have gone ignored. He and other professional firefighter union leaders met with the current Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez on August 13 for discussions on the budget but faced a frustrating two-hour conversation where Nuñez effectively told them nothing about what measures the funding bill would contain. “There’s been nothing, nothing at all,” Chabbouh told me, joking that Nuñez has been using the report to prop up a table for the past year. Nuñez justified his decision by saying that lawmakers in the National Assembly need to take a look at it before he shares it with union leaders and the public on September 8. Chabbouh said there’s no reason for the firefighter unions to hold off on striking given that there are zero guarantees that the budget will contain the resources they need. A union response is already scheduled, with a three-day occupation of Paris’s Place de la République to protest against government inaction planned to begin on September 26. More People One of the chief concerns firefighters have is a lack of manpower, especially when so many firefighters are facing exhaustion and injuries like smoke intoxication from prolonged exposure across days-long battles against the flames. By early August, most firefighters in Bouches-du-Rhône were already much more tired that they usually are, Laurent Guilloteau told me. Guilloteau, who is a subofficer in the SDIS and had a long career fighting fires on the front lines in the South of France, told me that the frequency and unprecedented geographic spread of the fires has contributed to that exhaustion. In his firehouse, ten people had already suffered from smoke intoxication. This year, Guilloteau told me, firefighters from Bouches-du-Rhône have already fought fires in the Pyrénées-Orientales, the Gironde, the Paris metropolitan region, the Alps, and the Var. That’s left nearly all of the firefighters in Guilloteau’s firehouse, which has forty-five professional fighters and around a hundred volunteers, close to the legal limits for work in a year. Professional firefighters in France, like all government employees, are capped at 1,607 hours a year, which works out to thirty-five hours a week. Across Bouches-du-Rhône there are around 1,400 professional firefighters. However, Guilloteau says that the General Confederation of Labor (CGT) union for the département has determined that they need to hire three hundred more professionals to “guarantee the safety of all citizens.” One concrete example of the dangers a lack of manpower can present comes from the ocean. The mistral — ocean winds that come howling off the seas at speeds of up to eighty miles per hour — can blow what would be manageable fires into deadly blazes, which race across the Mediterranean coast at up to four miles per hour. Firefighters in Bouches-du-Rhône have a “rule of 30.” When the outside temperature is over 30°C (80°F), when the wind speed reaches thirty kilometers per hour (18.6 miles per hour), and when humidity is around 30 percent, there’s a high chance of a fire breaking out. In conditions like these, the firefighters try to proactively combat potential fires by reinforcing the number of personnel and trucks they have ready to go across fire-sensitive areas. But when the wind comes, Guilloteau says there just aren’t enough firefighters to fight all the fires. Volunteer Your Firefighters The year 2026 is the first Bruno Ménard can remember when local-level authorities in each département denied requests to send their firefighters to other parts of France. This unprecedented geographical distribution of fires has left the départements skittish about sending much-needed personnel to other regions to fight the flames, said Ménard, who is president of the volunteer firefighters’ union. These two hundred thousand volunteers represent about three-quarters of France’s overall firefighting force. That seems like a lot, but Ménard explained that there’s a manpower shortage when it comes to the voluntary brigades too, even though they recruit between twenty and thirty thousand volunteers per year. There are a few reasons for that. But high on the list, Ménard says, is a sense of being let down that many volunteer firefighters feel after being on the job for a while. Demands like being available for a hundred hours a month, abysmally low pay of €0.80 an hour while on standby waiting to fight a fire, as well as active and ongoing training commitments, all contribute to pushing badly needed volunteer firefighters away from the calling. “It’s almost a second job,” Ménard told me. While the time commitments can be substantial and the physical dangers serious, volunteer firefighters don’t enjoy workplace protections that let them claim workers’ compensation for injuries sustained in the line of duty. They can even be fired from their day jobs if those injuries prevent them from doing their work. “It wears you out,” says Landes-based volunteer Hureaux. “We’re finding it harder and harder to keep our volunteer firefighters.” Volunteers, Hureaux adds, aren’t trying to replace professionals. The principle of signing up as a volunteer should mean that you contribute time when you have it. The trouble is that, with so much demand for firefighters right now and the consistent personnel shortages, they often feel obliged to show up so their comrades aren’t left with the burden. “Within a few years it weighs too heavy on people, and unfortunately they throw in the towel,” Hureaux said. “‘Okay, I quit.’” Despite this, the government’s latest concern to push through austerity measures means there’s no money to hire new firefighters even where there are professionals available who have completed the necessary training. At the same time, Ménard says, the government is refusing to even get around the table and look at volunteers’ demands. “If they don’t start negotiating, we’ll get out our atomic weapon,” Ménard said, pointing to a recent European Union directive that instructed member states to pay volunteer firefighters the same as professional ones. “If they don’t listen to us, we’ll demand they pay us the same amount,” Ménard promised, explaining that those figures were estimated at between €6–€8 billion additional spending per year. “We’ll blow up the public finances.”

articles.title: UAW Members Voting for International Officers
articles.author: Detroit DSA
articles.content: Delegates to the UAW Convention in June heard candidates for top offices. Any active member could run; there was no signature-gathering requirement as in some other unions. Photo: Jim West | jimwestphoto.com By Luis Feliz Leon and Jane Slaughter United Auto Workers members are voting by mail ballot for their top officers, for the second time in the union’s 91 years. Ballots went out August 21 and are due back by October 5. The contest will decide whether President Shawn Fain, who became famous for leading 2023’s Stand-Up Strike against the Big 3 automakers, will be able to continue the union’s about-face from its previous employer-friendly ways. William Hughes, a member of UAW Local 249 at Ford Kansas City, said the election is about maintaining the union’s momentum in winning gains for the membership. “During my 27 years in the union, I’ve never seen anything even close to the amount of gains that we’ve been getting in all these contracts — not just in the Big 3,” said Hughes. “I built seats before I came to Ford, and under no circumstances that I can recall would the parts sector ever strike these plants and try to really push for bigger contracts.” Fain was first elected in 2023 on a platform of “no corruption, no tiers, no concessions.” He is running on a record of successful contract fights at the Big 3 and elsewhere, and a pledge to keep organizing parts suppliers and nonunion auto plants in the South. His opponents have downplayed the gains made in the last three years, asserting that any president could have won them. Instead, they have focused on strife at union headquarters and unflattering reports issued by the federal monitor, Neil Barofsky, who was appointed in 2021 to oversee the union after massive corruption was uncovered and a dozen officers went to jail. NEW SMILES Fain’s strongest base of support is in locals where members have experienced the new willingness to fight management. JoAnna McClenathan is a senior designer at General Dynamics Electric Boat in Connecticut and a steering committee member of the reform network UAW Member Action , which is backing Fain. She credits Fain for opening up bargaining and creating a new Department of Bargaining Strategies that helped her local score a “record contract” with 30 percent raises. Fain set up that department to research employers and involve members in escalating campaigns. “During our contract fight last year, he came down and met with us, and he was a big reason we had the resources we did,” she said. “We had essentially been bargaining behind closed doors since the 1980s. For so long, a lot of us in our local felt powerless: this is what they’ve given us, so we’re just going to vote for this. Last year, the rank and file was able to use our voice and become more engaged, and that’s due to the new strategy.” Similarly at American Axle, an auto parts supplier in Three Rivers, Michigan, members are happy with the results of a two-week strike in June. They will be making $30 an hour by 2030, up from a top pay of $22. “We’re starting to see a change in the parking lot,” said bargaining committee member Jon Krause. “People are now able to buy cars that can get them to work. Some are looking to buy their first homes. We’ve seen a few people smiling that we haven’t seen smile in years.” Krause predicts Three Rivers members will vote for Fain’s United UAW slate. Legal services worker Brian Sullivan, a member of UAW Local 2325, said workers in his industry have set their sights on bargaining sector-wide. They were inspired by Fain’s industry-wide strategy with the automakers, he said: “We want a UAW leadership that’s going to back us as we take similarly big swings.” FIVE CHALLENGERS Fain’s five challengers spent most of the union’s presidential debate July 30 attacking him. They are Rich Boyer, vice president for the Stellantis Department; Tricia Geiger, an international servicing rep; Stellantis worker Brian Keller; Mack Truck worker Will Lehman; and Greg Mooney, recording secretary from Local 2147. Of the challengers, Boyer and Keller have the most name recognition. Keller won 14 percent of the vote in 2022 and spearheaded failed efforts to recall Fain last year. He finished fourth out of five candidates in his local union’s (Local 1248) delegate election this spring. Boyer and Fain ran on the same slate in the last election, as did Vice President Mike Booth and Secretary-Treasurer Margaret Mock, also now opposing Fain’s slate on their own slate, Integrity. Their differences have been the subject of long reports by the monitor. Fain accused Boyer of failing to enforce the contract at Stellantis and of responsibility for a new attendance program that members hated, as well as trying to secure union jobs for family members — standard practice in the old UAW. Boyer has consistently maintained that it’s the union’s job to enforce company attendance policies. In a video message to members about the 2023 contract ratification, he bemoaned the overuse of medical leave (FMLA) by people who “don’t want to do the work” and implied that plants would close if the union didn’t help fix attendance. The union’s executive board voted to relieve Boyer and Mock (who had also tried to put a family member on the payroll) of some of their assignments. Fain and other board members said Mock was using her office to block projects and retaliate against staffers she disliked. The monitor agreed with Boyer and Mock that their removal was “retaliation,” and they were reinstated. Earlier, the monitor had called Fain to lobby against the executive board’s December 2023 call for a ceasefire in Gaza. Fain angrily refused to back down, and he charges the monitor with having it in for him ever since. Barofsky accuses Fain of seeking favors for his fiancee and her sister. “The truth when it comes to Boyer is that I didn’t want him running the Stellantis Department because he wasn’t doing a good job for our members,” Fain told The Nation magazine. “I wouldn’t let him hire family members into UAW positions, and I wouldn’t stand by while he bargained concessions with Stellantis and failed to enforce our contract.” Boyer’s supporters say he is outspoken and a fighter. His main pledges in his campaign statement in the UAW magazine were to lower union dues to two hours a month, reduce the staff and salaries at union headquarters, and hire only from within the membership. Delegates at this summer’s convention voted to keep dues at 2.5 hours to build up the strike fund and provide resources for aggressive organizing and bargaining campaigns . The dueling ugly accusations have fed member cynicism, the prevailing attitude before 2023. Fain’s opponents are largely focused on the “infighting” among the leadership. “I don’t like the way [Fain] treats people,” said Jennifer Miller, recording secretary at Local 1700 near Detroit, who backs Boyer. “I don’t like the arrogance of him. I don’t think he deserves credit for everything he says he’s done.” In the last election, Fain, who was running against then-President Ray Curry, benefited from a powerful anti-incumbent sentiment, stemming from years of frustration with concessions, plant closures, and corruption at the union’s top levels. This time, he won’t have that advantage. JJ Barbosa, a millwright at Stellantis’s Jeep plant in Toledo, has backed Keller, a prolific Facebook presence, in all three of his runs. He sees Keller as tenacious and consistent, and he is “disgusted that there are still tiers.” He says all the incumbents are guilty of “cronyism and nepotism.” MOMENTUM In interviews with members across the union, it was common to hear that they were impressed that Fain showed up at locals to talk with members and supported their contract fights. Carlos Gonzalez-Rios, a 27-year worker at the General Motors engine plant in Buffalo, New York, said he met Fain twice. He rattled off a few of the gains he’s seen, including a pay increase of 25 percent. “We got COLA back,” he said. “We don’t have endless temporary workers for five or six years.” He also cited the union’s win at Volkswagen in Tennessee, where workers voted to join the UAW and won a first contract earlier this year — becoming the first unionized foreign-owned auto assembly plant in the South. What’s at stake in the election, Gonzalez-Rios argues, is whether this momentum will continue. “I’d rather go with the guy that’s been proven and has the leadership skills that brought us what we have right now,” he said. “And we still have issues that we are working towards — we want health care for all at GM after retirement.” “I’ve held people accountable and that pisses some people off, I understand that,” said Fain during the presidential debate. “But running on a platform of ‘the monitor said this or that,’ that’s not going to deliver for the membership.” CHANGING ALLIANCES The union’s 400,000 active members and nearly 600,000 retirees will be electing all 14 positions on the union’s International Executive Board. Fain’s United UAW slate, which is contesting 13 of the seats, includes candidates who ran against him in the last election as members of the “Administration Caucus” that had run the union since the 1940s and overseen multiple waves of concessions in recent decades. Some have been won over by the impressive contract results that Fain’s bold approach has achieved; others may be inclined to go with the one in power. In early August, three ex-UAW presidents, Ray Curry, Rory Gamble, and Ron Gettelfinger, attempted to resurrect the old ruling caucus by releasing a letter backing Geiger, Mock, and other Fain opponents. Fain shot back, reminding members of Gettelfinger’s “sellout deal” in 2007 that cut wages in half for new-hires and created the two-tier system. Four regional directors on Fain’s slate are running unopposed: Mark DePaoli in Region 1A, Mike Miller in Region 6, Tim Smith in Region 8, and Brandon Mancilla in Region 9A. The other five director seats and three vice president seats are all contested, as is the secretary-treasurer slot. Candidates need a majority to avoid a run-off, and votes will be tabulated October 6. Luis Feliz Leon is a staff writer and organizer with Labor Notes. Jane Slaughter is a former editor of Labor Notes and co-author of Secrets of a Successful Organizer. This article originally appeared in Labor Notes . UAW Members Voting for International Officers was originally published in The Detroit Socialist on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

articles.title: Colombia’s Far Right Sees an Earthquake as an Opportunity
articles.author: Cruz Bonlarron Martínez
articles.content: On August 10, western Colombia was rocked by a 7.8 magnitude earthquake. Images of collapsed buildings and ordinary citizens organizing to remove the rubble quickly circulated on social media and through news agencies. Cali, the region’s largest city, quickly became the week’s trending topic. This came just three days after the country’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella had taken power in a highly divisive and militarized spectacle held at a military base in the city, which voted overwhelmingly for his leftist competitor Iván Cepeda. Now after the earthquake, Cali and western Colombia are taking center stage in the administration’s reversal of Gustavo Petro’s redistributive policies and its attempt to refound Colombia as a bastion of far-right politics. The Initial Response Instead of coordinating international support for those affected by the earthquake, de la Espriella’s foreign ministry sent shockwaves through much of the diplomatic community by releasing a statement that legitimized Israel’s occupation of Syrian territory in the Golan Heights. This made it one of only two countries to do so — the other being the United States. This was a decision that seemed severely out of place even to many of the government’s supporters. It unnecessarily isolated the country from the international community at a time when it faced one of the most vulnerable moments in its recent history. Simultaneously, the foreign ministry also issued a similar statement recognizing Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara and freezing diplomatic relations with the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic. At home, de la Espriella’s colossal ego dominated the initial response to the disaster, with the newly inaugurated president waving and blowing kisses to the audience just before announcing the death toll and damage caused by the earthquake. Ironically, because de la Espriella abstained from conducting a formal transition of power for the first time in the country’s recent democratic history, the director of the Colombian disaster agency, Javier Pava, was still a leftist appointed by outgoing President Petro. Pava and his team had to deal with the uncomfortable task of handling the initial response and dispatching government workers to the site of the disaster in cooperation with a hostile administration. In the midst of the crisis, de la Espriella also began bombing National Liberation Army encampments in the Catatumbo region on the other side of the country, reportedly causing civilian casualties and damage to infrastructure in the region. The bombing was criticized by various members of the opposition for disproportionate use of force and violations of international humanitarian law while the country was immersed in a humanitarian crisis. The bombing also occurred in parallel with an announcement from the United States Secretary of War Pete Hegseth that US troops would be involved in future military operations on Colombian soil. Debris from damaged structures litters the Pampalinda neighborhood in Buenaventura, Colombia. (Courtesy Gilberto Villaseñor Quiles) One of the most jaw-dropping moments of the government’s reaction to the earthquake was the failure to ask for international assistance to rescue those trapped in the rubble. Of all people, it was El Salvador’s right-wing President Nayib Bukele who revealed that the Colombian government had rejected his initial offer to provide a rescue team. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum also emphasized that Mexico was ready to send their own disaster team at a moment’s notice but had not received a response. After mounting pressure for a statement on how the government planned to ask for international help, the government stated that it would only receive rescue teams from Ecuador, Israel, the United States, and El Salvador, all of which are governed by far-right allies. Government officials claimed that, while they were open to receiving help in the form of supplies from other countries, only these four states had the certificates necessary to conduct disaster relief operations. Afro-Colombian and Indigenous Mutual Aid The regions hardest hit by the earthquake are ones where Afro-Colombian and indigenous peoples make up a large part, and in many cases a majority, of the population. For instance, in the department of Chocó, the department home to the epicenter of the earthquake, nearly 95 percent of the population identifies as Afro-Colombian or indigenous. As with many other countries of the Americas, including the United States, in Colombia black and indigenous communities constitute some of the most marginalized and oppressed communities due to the lasting impacts of colonization and slavery. Colombians assess the damage in Buenaventura. (Courtesy Gilberto Villaseñor Quiles) In Colombia, such marginalization is exacerbated by the concentration of these communities in rural areas where there is a weak state presence in the provision of services and where the armed conflict continues to have an impact. These issues were key to the Petro administration’s peace negotiations, and they were part of the reason why regions with large indigenous and Afro-Colombian populations voted overwhelmingly for Iván Cepeda in both the first and second round of this year’s presidential election. Afro-Colombian and indigenous communities were more vulnerable to the destruction the earthquake caused because the infrastructure that exists in those communities is already precarious. However, the communities themselves began to organize directly for support and mutual aid. Colombian women stand in their now roofless home, one of over 10,000 affected by the recent earthquake. (Courtesy Gilberto Villaseñor Quiles) In the capital Bogotá, organizations ranging from large indigenous federations to Afro-Colombian cultural associations made calls to their networks to donate what they could to provide a lifeline for those displaced by the earthquake. Even Shakira took part in the effort, pledging to donate over a million US dollars to Chocó and publicly criticizing the Colombian state’s historical abandonment of the region. Afro-Colombian and indigenous members of Congress have created funds to directly reach the communities affected by the earthquake. Óscar Benavides, a representative for the leftist Afro-Colombian Libres Party, has gained national attention for his early role in raising funds and supplies for communities on the Pacific coast of the country. Despite attacks from the right-wing media, Benavides has reportedly raised over $100,000 for the relief effort. He has also shipped thirteen trucks full of supplies to the region and conducted visits there with the Indigenous representative and former vice-presidential candidate, Aida Quilcué. Rebuilding in Buenaventura In Buenaventura, one of the cities most affected by the earthquake and the country’s largest port on the Pacific coast, 82 percent of the city’s population was already living in conditions of extreme poverty prior to the earthquake. The city has a population of about 433,000 people, with the vast majority living in its urban core. Eighty-nine percent of the city’s population are Afro descendent, and 1 percent are considered indigenous. María Eugenia Mosquera, who works with the organization Conpazcol, told us about the impact of the disaster: Unfortunately, whenever these disasters happen, it’s the working-class neighborhoods that are most affected, right? Where there are fewer conditions for a decent life, and these were precisely the homes that were most destroyed. And sadly, sometimes the focus is more on those who have and not on those who don’t. Conpazcol is an organization of human rights defenders and victims of Colombia’s armed conflict that works closely with Afro-Colombian, indigenous, and campesino communities in different parts of Colombia and has worked for years in Buenaventura. In the days since the earthquake, the organization has been trying to understand the ways in which different communities have been impacted while also seeking to ensure that earthquake aid is distributed to people and families that need help. While their president curries favor with the US and Israel, ordinary Colombians aid in disaster relief — and show solidarity with Palestinians. (Courtesy Gilberto Villaseñor Quiles) The Buenaventura mayor’s office recently published the following preliminary statistics regarding the earthquake’s impact: twenty-seven dead; 476 people injured; 10,148 families affected; 10,148 homes impacted; and 954 homes destroyed. These figures will very likely continue to rise as authorities are able to more clearly account for the damage caused by the earthquake. It’s probable that many more families were impacted, since multiple families often occupy a single home. Mosquera expressed concern about the reaction of the new Colombian government: The current president is more interested in war and extractive industries than actually thinking about what’s happening here. After the earthquake, all he’s done is arrive, take pictures, laugh, do things that aren’t appropriate for the situation, and he hasn’t provided the necessary response. Several Colombian officials have engaged in controversial actions and statements during visits to Buenaventura in the aftermath of the earthquake. President de la Espriella’s visit on August 16 was particularly controversial, because he threw soccer balls printed with propaganda from the recent electoral campaign promoting his own political party at earthquake victims. The situation reminded observers of the moment when Donald Trump threw paper towels at victims of Hurricane Maria in Puerto Rico in 2017. Silvia Estupiñán, a community leader from the neighborhood of Pampalinda in Buenaventura, was not impressed: The new government is out of touch with the disaster in the territory. It needs better guidance, because coming to Buenaventura or visiting other areas to hand out soccer balls is an insult to the people. It’s disrespectful and lacks professional ethics. Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara made headlines when he toured the earthquake damage with the mayor of Buenaventura. He said that the government would get the wood and cement, while the people of the area would “provide the labor themselves and fix it in two minutes.” Critics argued that it was insensitive for Lara to claim that the poorest residents of Buenaventura would be able to rebuild their houses almost immediately. Profit Over People The earthquake has revealed two contrasting models of disaster response in Colombia, corresponding to the political divisions that separated the country in June’s elections: a response from capital and a response from the people. De la Espriella’s administration has used the crisis as an opportunity to consolidate its ideological model and mold Colombia in the image of the global far right, fully aligning the country with Washington even if it means leaving citizens under the rubble and isolating the country from the rest of the world. It looks as if the reconstruction effort in the coming months will serve as a key part of the spectacle of capital accumulation in the territories destroyed by the earthquake, territories that overwhelmingly voted for Petro and Cepeda. However, the crisis following the earthquake has revealed another model of disaster response, one based upon solidarity and collective organizing. As Mosquera remarks: We have always said that international solidarity is crucial for the affected territories. First, it raises awareness. Second, it provides support . . . because amidst the crisis caused by the earthquake, there are also issues of protection. The historical abandonment by the Colombian state means that communities in Buenaventura and Chocó already have experience organizing themselves in the face of marginalization and adversity. This experience will be essential to survival as de la Espriella continues to implement an agenda that favors capital over life itself.

articles.title: Israel kills three in airstrike on Jenin
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: The Israeli Army announced on Friday, August 28 that it launched a drone strike in the northern West Bank city of Jenin, killing three Palestinian resistance fighters. It added that Qais Bitawi, whom it described as a Hamas operative in the dismantled Jenin Brigade, was among the fatalities. The other two slain men were identified as Basel Turkman and Ahmad Yaqoub Turkman, according to local media outlets which also reported that the bodies of the three Palestinians were confiscated by the Israeli forces. The deadly attack marks the first Israeli airstrike in the occupied West Bank in 10 months. It was also carried out as part of Israel’s extensive military operations in the occupied territory that started in January 2025. Read more: After the “Iron Wall”: Israel launches another large-scale operation in northern West Bank Palestinian resistance groups respond While the Israeli forces claimed that Bitawi was affiliated with Hamas, the Palestinian Islamic Jihad issued a statement on Friday, declaring that the three men were fighters in its military wing, the Saraya al-Quds Brigades. The movement denounced the assault as a “cowardly assassination”, asserting that “it will remain steadfast on the path of jihad and resistance until liberation and return.” The Palestinian resistance movement Hamas issued a statement , affirming that “this heinous crime will only be met with more anger and confrontation, as the West Bank will remain a source of revolutionaries and heroism.” The movement held the Israeli occupation “fully responsible for the repercussions of this strike, the escalating crimes, and the continuation of its brutal policy” that involves killing and terrorizing the Palestinian people, and demolishing their houses. It also called on “the Palestinian people in Jenin and other West Bank governorates to escalate all forms of resistance and disrupt the enemy’s security calculations.”

articles.title: Canada vs. Trump: Is this a trade war or something bigger?
articles.author: Rania Khalek
articles.content: Trump torched trade talks with Canada last week after demanding veto power over Canada’s own infrastructure spending and its ability to make deals with other countries. Toronto-based writer and geopolitical analyst Justin Podur tells Rania Khalek and Zoe Alexandra Washington’s demands went well beyond the terms of the USMCA (formerly NAFTA) into “total annexation-style stuff” before the Trump administration slapped 50% tariffs on $20 billion in Canadian goods, everything from dairy and alcohol to hockey equipment. Podur explains what Prime Minister Mark Carney’s “dollar for dollar” retaliation really means for two deeply unequal, deeply integrated economies; why a tens-of-billions-of-dollar F-35 deal is still quietly moving forward as both countries claim they’re at “war”; and why saying no to Trump has become cool across the Canadian political spectrum. He unpacks what this trade war actually reveals: a declining US empire bullying its closest allies, now that pushing around rivals like Iran and China isn’t working. articles.title: Babies are being held in ICE detention in Texas with Rep. Joaquin Castro
articles.author: Rania Khalek
articles.content: “The commodification of child imprisonment” under Donald Trump is making CoreCivic and GEO Group executives even richer, Rep. Joaquin Castro tells Rania Khalek and Zoe Alexandra. The Democrat representing Texas’s 20th Congressional District says babies as young as two months old are being held in ICE detention, and parents are being coerced into helping entrap their own children, all while private prison giants profit off every kid DHS locks up. Castro breaks down what he’s witnessed inside facilities like the Dilley “trailer prison,” and the explosion of 287(g) agreements turning local police departments into DHS henchmen. But what about the Democrats still voting to fund ICE despite the horrors it’s perpetrating? And can US voters expect real accountability for the mass deportation machine if Castro’s party retakes the House in November? articles.title: China saw this coming: Why Trump’s Iran sanctions won’t work with Dr. Ken Hammond
articles.author: Rania Khalek
articles.content: Beijing just proved the limits of Washington’s sanctions machine. As US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent rolls out “Operation Economic Outcast,” China is doing what almost no other country in the world can: refusing to comply with US sanctions on Iran. Dr. Ken Hammond, professor of East Asian and Global History at New Mexico State University, joins Rania Khalek and Zoe Alexandra to unpack how Trump’s promised “economic D-Day” is running headfirst into a wall, as Beijing shields Chinese companies from “illegitimate” US sanctions and continues to buy up to 90% of Iran’s sanctioned crude oil exports. Hammond explains why Trump’s bullying barely registers in Beijing, pointing to years of stockpiling oil reserves, diversifying suppliers, and building BRICS-based alternatives to dollar-dominated trade. China hawks in Congress are furious that while a Chinese tanker and a Hong Kong shipping firm got hit, Chinese banks were left untouched — a decision reportedly tied to Xi Jinping’s upcoming White House visit, where Hammond says “rare earths” will be the buzzword amid ongoing US-China trade tensions. It all points to China no longer needing to bend the knee to Washington. And with reports of Chinese satellite intelligence, MANPADS, and chip technology reaching Iran’s military-industrial sector, Beijing is signaling just how far it’s willing to go to keep the US empire in check. articles.title: Dolly Parton, Hayden Panettiere, and what Hollywood owes women
articles.author: Rania Khalek
articles.content: Rania Khalek and Zoe Alexandra honor Dolly Parton: working-class feminist icon, country music legend and lifelong advocate for the disenfranchised, as the world mourns her death Tuesday at the age of 80. They pay tribute to the songwriter who immortalized the fight for workplace dignity waged by 9 to 5, the National Association of Working Women; the Imagination Library founder and philanthropist who used $10 million in royalties from Whitney Houston’s “I Will Always Love You” (which she wrote) to invest in a historically Black Nashville neighborhood; and the human rights warrior who stood by the queer community decades before it was popular or professionally safe to do so — during the height of the 1980s AIDS crisis. Zoe and Rania also pay tribute to Hayden Panettiere, star of Heroes and Nashville who started acting as a baby before roles on One Life to Live and Guiding Light , who was found dead last week at just 36. Her memoir reveals a harrowing pattern of patriarchal exploitation: fired by Neutrogena for speaking out about postpartum depression, given “happy pills” as a child on the red carpet, and pushed into predatory encounters with powerful figures in Hollywood. Rania and Zoe connect Panettiere’s story to Britney Spears, Amanda Bynes, and Demi Lovato — asking what it means that even the most famous, beautiful, and wealthy white women are chewed up and discarded by capitalism’s total disregard for the people who make its profits. articles.title: Right-wing attack on university in West Bengal sparks mass protests
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Massive protests were organized in cities and towns across the Indian state of West Bengal on Wednesday, August 26 protesting against the rising right-wing attacks on the educational institutions and activists. This was the third such protest action taken since the August 20 midnight attack on the university by the ultra right-wing and Hindu supremacist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS)-affiliated student organization Akhil Bhartiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP). Several students and teachers were injured in the attack and university property was vandalized. Students have lodged accusations that the security forces were unresponsive, while elected members of the state legislative assembly from the ruling BJP were directly involved. ABVP-BJP-RSS goons arrived on bikes at midnight and unleashed violence inside Jadavpur University campus, attacking students with weapons, vandalising union rooms, throwing stones and bricks and setting fire to students’ belongings. pic.twitter.com/C7193wb1rW — CPI (M) (@cpimspeak) August 19, 2026 In the recent protests, activists expressed their solidarity with the students of Jadavpur University and demanded that all those involved in the attack be held accountable. The protesters also demanded action against the forces involved in acts of vandalism against progressive and left symbols in the state. A wave of attacks have swept the state since the BJP came into power in the state earlier this year. Protests were called by various left parties and student organizations in the state including the Students’ Federation of India (SFI), All India Students’ Federation (AISF), All India Students’ Association (AISA) among others. The left and progressive student groups had led a massive march from the JU campus to the city on August 22 , a day after the attack. They carried out a much bigger protest march on August 24 as well . The Left is the target The BJP-RSS-ABVP and similar right wing groups now backed by the ruling dispensation in the state have alleged that JU and other prominent universities have become a den of “anti-national” activities and demand the removal of progressive and left teaching staff and ban on the activities of the left leaning student unions. Before storming the university campus on August 20 they had carried out several attempts to demolish a statue of Lenin just outside the campus and vandalized several other statues in different parts of the state. Reports also indicate that several left and progressive activists have been killed and injured in targeted attacks. The attacks on the universities and the left activists in West Bengal is similar to the attacks carried out by the same forces in the rest of the country. Universities such as Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) and Jamia Milia Islamia (JMI), both in the capital New Delhi, have been repeatedly targeted by the right-wing assailants in the past decade for their vocal opposition to sectarian and pro-capital policies of the BJP. In addition to physical injuries, some activists have also faced charges. The mainstream media in India, as in the past incidents, called the attacks at JU a “clash between ABVP and SFI.” BJP leader and chief minister of the state Suvendu Adhikari, instead of condemning the attack and taking action against the assailants, ordered an “investigation” into “anti-national activities” on the campuses. Commenting on the attacks on JU, Vijay Prashad, historian and director of the Tricontinental Institute of Social Research compared it with the attacks on JNU calling it a fight “that will not find an easy solution.” He wrote on his social media page that the real motive of the right wing behind these repeated attacks is to destroy the left in the country. Suchetna Chattopadhyay who teaches history at JU called the attack an example of “textbook neoliberal fascism of our times.” She alleged that the attack on August 20 was a part of the larger and more systematic attacks on the left, an attempt to instill fear so that all kinds of opposition to its policies designed to serve the interest of big capital is silenced.

articles.title: Military government in Guinea-Bissau seeks to reshape political system with referendum
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: Guinea-Bissau is set to vote on a new constitution on Sunday, August 30, in a referendum that could alter the country’s political system and strengthen the powers of the presidency. The referendum comes nine months after the military seized control. The crisis traces back to November 23, 2025, when Guinea-Bissau held presidential and parliamentary elections. Both incumbent President Umaro Sissoco Embaló and opposition candidate Fernando Dias da Costa claimed victory. Before the electoral commission could release provisional results, the military intervened on November 26, one day ahead of the announcement suspending the vote count and arresting opposition figures including PAIGC leader Domingos Simões Pereira and PRS’s Francisco da Costa. General Horta N’Tam was installed as transitional president. What the new constitution would change The draft marks a major rebalancing of power. Currently, the parliamentary majority largely determines the government. Under the proposed system, the president would gain authority to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and ministers, chair the Council of Ministers, restructure ministries, and dissolve Parliament under certain conditions, including once per term without needing Council of State approval. The draft also shrinks Parliament from 102 to 61 seats and cuts electoral constituencies from 29 to 12, changes analysts warn could disadvantage locally-rooted parties and consolidate power among larger blocs. Opposition says referendum risks consolidating military-backed rule Zizwe Tchiguka of the African Party for the Independence of Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde (PAIGC), speaking about the political crisis and the proposed constitutional changes to BreakThrough News, described the November 2025 military intervention as a “fake coup” designed to prevent the opposition from taking power. The coup is not seen in the same breath as the coups in the AES fight for sovereignty rather than its a safeguarding of the ruling class interests. “The day before the election results were supposed to be announced last November 26, 2025,” Tchiguka said, “the previous illegal president, Umar Sissoko Mbalo, staged a fake coup d’etat.” He questioned why the former president was able to leave the country while opposition figures were arrested. “How could you have a coup d’etat but you could be interviewed by the press and then you could go and get on a plane and leave the country?” he asked. “But the opposition candidates are arrested at the same time.” According to Tchiguka, the arrests included PAIGC leader Domingos Simões Pereira and Francisco da Costa of the Social Renewal Party (PRS), which had participated in the opposition coalition. Domingos Simões Pereira of the PAIGC. Photo: Communist Party of Portugal His concern is that the proposed constitution could fundamentally alter the balance between the presidency, the prime minister and Parliament. “The military regime is trying to change the constitution so that the person who is elected as the President can make the prime minister powerless, null and void,” Tchiguka said, describing this as one of the key features of the proposed constitutional arrangement. He argued that the changes could be used to ensure that an administration acceptable to the military establishment retains effective control even if opposition forces perform strongly in the elections. “So that if they could manipulate the election, they could prevent the opposition party, which is led by Domingos Simões Pereira, from having any power,” he said. Tchiguka further argued that control over Parliament is particularly important because of Simões Pereira’s position within the legislative system. “If you know he’s the president of the parliament, he’s the president of the Legislative Assembly, he would be the second most powerful person in the government,” he said. “What they’re trying to do is to position the person who they can have put in power by a bogus election,” he added, “to make it so that he will be powerless to do anything.” Tchiguka also challenges the legality and timing of the referendum, arguing that constitutional changes should not be undertaken so close to an election. “This idea of having a referendum on the constitution is illegal because ECOWAS, Economic Community of West African States, has a law that you cannot change the constitution no earlier than six months prior to the election date,” he said. He similarly says that Guinea-Bissau’s own legal framework prevents constitutional amendments or a referendum within six months of an election. “This is the scenario that we’re faced with,” he said, “to try to change the constitution this coming Sunday, August the 30th, and to try to set up another election on December the 6th.” Opposition calls for restoration of constitutional order The opposition and allies internationally have called for the restoration of constitutional institutions, the release of political prisoners, the reopening of party headquarters that were shut, and guarantees for political activity. The International Network in Solidarity with Guinea-Bissau is also calling for soldiers to return to the barracks and for conditions that allow political activists to participate freely in the electoral process. Tchiguka said opposition forces are urging citizens not to participate in what they regard as an illegitimate electoral process. “We’re telling the masses of people in Guinea-Bissau, do not go out. Don’t participate in this false election process,” he said. But he also described a second strategy should the referendum and subsequent elections proceed. “Even if they manage to get the people to come out and vote, our next plan is to put pressure on the government, that is the illegal government,” he said. The objective, he explained, would be to ensure that the elected National Assembly retains its constitutional role. “What we’re saying is that even if they manage to pass this bogus constitution, you still have this legislative assembly that should be in place,” Tchiguka said. He pointed to the continued occupation of opposition party headquarters and restrictions on the National Assembly as evidence, in his view, that constitutional institutions have yet to be fully restored. “They presently occupy the headquarters of the PAIGC,” he said, “and they presently have the People’s National Assembly locked out of the assembly building.” The vote unfolds with unresolved questions over the transitional government’s legitimacy, the uncertified November 2025 results, and the fairness of December’s elections. Tchiguka also adds that Embaló remains politically active and could benefit from a path back to power, part of the opposition’s broader reading of the crisis. He concludes that the situation represents “a real desperate situation for the illegal military regime to try to stay in power.”

articles.title: Health activists in India demand affordable breast cancer treatments
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: Health activists and public health experts in India are pushing for affordable breast cancer treatments as the Kerala High Court continues to hear a case originally filed in 2022. The case and the surrounding advocacy concern access to the medications ribociclib and abemaciclib – both of which have demonstrated significant benefits for patients with early-stage breast cancer but remain prohibitively expensive for a large part of the population. Breast cancer represents a true public health crisis in India, noted the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatment. In 2024 , of the 780,000 new cancer cases among women, breast cancer accounted for 237,000 diagnoses. India also has a notable survival gap compared to other countries: five-year survival stands at 65.7%, compared to 87.3% in high-income countries. “The price of the treatment is one of the biggest barriers,” the Working Group noted. “Ribociclib costs around 75,000 rupees (approximately USD 786) a month. A three-year course can therefore cost close to 27 lakh rupees (approximately USD 28,300). Abemaciclib costs roughly 48,000–95,000 rupees (approximately USD 500-995) a month. Such prices put these medicines beyond the reach of most families.” Members of the working group stress that the high cost stems from the treatments’ market positioning. “Ribociclib and abemaciclib remain available mainly as expensive branded medicines and are not routinely available through government support programs,” they point out, with a significant impact on rural and poor patients. “Nearly 100,000 women are dying of breast cancer every year. If that is not a public health emergency, what is?” asked co-convener of the Working Group Jyotsna Singh . “The woman who first approached the Court died before she could get the medicine she needed. Many more women have died while this case has continued.” Calls to invoke Patents Act safeguards to ensure treatment accessibility Activists are urging the Indian government to trigger safeguards under the Indian Patents Act, including compulsory licensing, to expand access to ribociclib and abemaciclib. They say this should be done swiftly and decisively, especially after the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) submitted a counter affidavit containing contradictory information, adding a new layer of complication. At one point in the brief, the Working Group warns, CDSCO claims ribociclib is approved for the same indications as palbociclib, a generically available and thus cheaper medicine. While the two are both used in the treatment of advanced cases of cancer, ribociclib has additionally demonstrated notable benefits in early-stage cases. This means the treatment can help prevent cancer cells from returning and becoming metastatic, “when the disease is much harder to cure,” the Working Group pointed out. The formulation in CDSCO’s submission risks implying the same benefits can be expected from palbociclib. “This is not a minor discrepancy,” the Working Group insists. “It risks misleading the Court into believing that the cheaper palbociclib can replace ribociclib for early-stage breast cancer, when the data placed before the court by CDSCO itself says otherwise.” “A drug regulator has a responsibility to place clear and accurate information before the Court, particularly when women’s access to life-saving treatment is at stake,” emphasized Gargeya Telakapalli, co-coordinator of the Working Group. “The government must correct the record and act urgently to make ribociclib and abemaciclib affordable, including through compulsory licensing where monopoly pricing continues to block access.” Read more: India’s newly amended patent rules threaten affordable medicines in the Global South Renowned oncologist Dr. R. Ravi Kannan, Director of Cachar Cancer Hospital, submitted a court opinion echoing many of these observations and further clarifying the different profiles of palbociclib, ribociclib, and abemaciclib – calling for wider availability of the latter two. “Every advancement that safely reduces recurrence risk is vital,” he wrote, “because each relapse means additional financial burden on the family and risk of poverty, with the loss of cure and a return to only palliative options.” “Generic entry has historically been the single most reliable lever for expanding access to targeted cancer therapies in resource-limited settings, and there is no clinical reason to expect abemaciclib and ribociclib to be an exception,” he added. “The government cannot keep treating access to breast cancer medicines as an ordinary pricing dispute,” Singh concluded ahead of the next hearing, scheduled for September 3, 2026. “Women need the best available treatment when it can still save their lives.” People’s Health Dispatch is a fortnightly bulletin published by the People’s Health Movement and Peoples Dispatch .
